title: What is the currency of Cambodia? Riel symbol and code
summary: Cambodia currency explained: the riel, its symbol and code, and why US dollars are used there too. Grey moves money at a fair rate. Send yours today.
body_markdown:
Before a trip to Siem Reap, you look up Cambodia’s currency and find that it’s the riel. Then a friend who has been there tells you to bring US dollars, and the first ATM you use hands out dollars, not riel. Both are true, and how the two currencies fit together decides how you pay, what change you get back and where you lose money to poor rates. This guide covers the riel, its symbol and code, why dollars circulate alongside it, and how to spend and send money in Cambodia.


The currency of Cambodia is the Cambodian riel, symbol ៛ and code KHR. In practice, US dollars are widely used across Cambodia, especially for larger purchases, while riel is often used for small change. Many prices are quoted in dollars in tourist areas.


## What is the currency of Cambodia?


The currency of Cambodia is the Cambodian riel, but US dollars are used alongside it every day, so most visitors end up handling both. The riel is the national currency, and the National Bank of Cambodia is its sole issuer. The dollar isn't issued by Cambodia at all, yet it's what most ATMs dispense and what many hotels, restaurants and shops use to set their prices.


In practice, the two currencies split the work:


- US dollars cover larger payments: hotel rooms, tours, restaurant bills and most prices in cities and tourist areas.
- Riel cover small purchases such as street food and tuk-tuk rides, and they’re the everyday currency in rural areas.


There are no US coins in circulation in Cambodia, so any change smaller than a dollar comes back in riel. That's why a visitor's wallet is usually a mix: dollar notes for the main payment and a stack of riel for the change. Near the Thai border, shops may also accept Thai baht, though usually at a poor rate.


The rest of this guide covers the riel itself, how the dollar became so common, and what to do with both when you travel or send money.


## The Cambodian riel: Symbol and code


The Cambodian riel uses the symbol ៛ and the ISO currency code KHR. You'll see ៛ on price lists and signs in Cambodia, while KHR is the code used by banks, exchange apps and currency converters. The[National Bank of Cambodia](https://www.nbc.gov.kh/english/about_the_bank/faqs.php) says it is the sole issuer of the Khmer riel, the national currency.


The riel is nominally divided into 100 sen, but sen aren't used in everyday life. Riel banknotes run from 100 riel up to 100,000 riel, and because a single riel is worth so little, prices in riel are usually written in the thousands.


A US dollar buys roughly 4,000 riel, and shops commonly round to that figure when they work out change. Rates move, so check the day's rate before you exchange money. The National Bank of Cambodia describes its approach as a managed floating exchange rate, where the rate is allowed to move within a band.


That high number of riel per dollar is why the currency appears on lists of[the least valuable currencies](https://grey.co/blog/least-valuable-currency) . Such a ranking only counts how many units buy one dollar. It doesn't measure how strong an economy is, and a low-value currency can reflect history, such as past hyperinflation, rather than current conditions.


## Why US dollars are used in Cambodia


US dollars are used in Cambodia because people lost confidence in the riel after years of upheaval, and a large inflow of dollars in the early 1990s made the dollar the easier currency to trust and spend. The National Bank of Cambodia's own[research paper on dollarisation](https://www.nbc.gov.kh/download_files/publication/others_eng/NoteMD117-14_article_dollarization.pdf) says dollarisation did not result from a policy decision. It built up as shocks wore down trust in the riel.


Year What happened


1975 The Khmer Rouge destroyed the financial system and decided not to issue a new currency


1980 The central bank was re-established and the riel became legal tender again


1990 to 1992 Central bank financing of the budget fuelled a sharp riel devaluation and three-digit hyperinflation


1991 to 1992 The UN transitional operation, which cost USD 1.7 billion, brought large dollar inflows


1993 onward The dollar has been widely used since 1993, and it stayed in use after stability returned in 1999


‍


Memory of that hyperinflation is why the habit lasted. The same paper put foreign currency at 97.3% of bank deposits at the end of 2006, which shows how far people had moved their savings into dollars. The central bank has since encouraged wider use of the riel, so the balance may have shifted, but the day-to-day split described above still holds for most visitors.


In practice, prices are often quoted in dollars, and you can pay in either currency. If a drink costs $2.50 and you pay with a $5 note, the change might come back as $2 and 2,000 riel, at the common rounded rate of 4,000 riel to the dollar.

## Money tips for travellers in Cambodia


For most trips, carry small, undamaged US dollar notes for everyday spending, a little riel for small purchases, and a card for the places that accept one. Cash is the main way to pay in much of the country, so a few habits protect you from the usual losses:


- **Bring clean, untorn dollar notes.** Banks, money changers and shops can refuse notes with tears or heavy marks, and larger notes are the hardest to use. Check yours before you fly.
- **Carry small bills.** Tuk-tuk drivers and street vendors often can't break a large note, so $1, $5 and $10 notes go further than a $50 or $100.
- **Keep some riel.** You'll want it for motorbike taxis, snacks and small shops, and it has little value outside Cambodia, so spend what's left before you go.
- **Expect dollars from ATMs.** Most ATMs dispense US dollars, often in large notes, and some charge a fee per withdrawal. Read the screen before you confirm.
- **Count your change.** In busy tourist areas, riel change is sometimes short. A quick check takes seconds.
- **Compare money changers.**[Tourism Cambodia](https://www.tourismcambodia.com/tripplanner/general-travel-information/time-money-banking.htm) says money changers generally give slightly better rates than banks, so compare a few before you swap.


Cards work in a narrower set of places. The same source says they're accepted at upscale hotels, shops and restaurants in the major tourist towns and generally not elsewhere, and that most businesses that take cards add a fee of 2% to 4%. Ask before you pay, and keep cash as your backup.


Your own bank is the other place money leaks. Many cards add a foreign transaction fee on purchases in another currency, and[how to avoid foreign transaction fees](https://grey.co/blog/avoid-foreign-transaction-fees) explains what to look for. Because many Cambodian prices are in dollars, a[dollar card](https://grey.co/cards) can pay those without a currency conversion, while riel prices are a different currency and may trigger a conversion or cross-border fee depending on the card.

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the currency of Cambodia?


The currency of Cambodia is the Cambodian riel (KHR). US dollars circulate alongside it and are widely used for larger purchases and in tourist areas, while riel is used mostly for small amounts and change.


### What is the riel symbol?


The riel symbol is ៛. You may see it on price lists in Cambodia, while banks and currency converters use the code KHR instead.


### What is the currency code for Cambodia?


The currency code is KHR. Use it in currency converters, bank forms and exchange apps when you look up the Cambodian riel.


### Can I use US dollars in Cambodia?


Yes. Dollars are widely accepted in cities and tourist areas, and most ATMs dispense them. Change under a dollar comes back in riel, and torn or heavily marked notes may be refused, so carry clean, small bills.


### Should I carry riel?


Yes, carry a small amount for tuk-tuks, snacks and small shops, where riel is the usual currency. It has little value outside Cambodia, so spend or exchange what's left before you leave.
